transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it wasn’t my idea to come here, I’ll tell you that right now. I’ve been on the trucks for years, I'm an EMT, and you get to know how the equipment has to be, how it breathes, almost. But my lieutenant... they, uh, they sent me here because of what happened at the station. 

I was down in the bay, right? And the airway bags—the ones we use for intubation and oxygen, they have all the non-rebreather masks and the O2 tanks in them—they just weren't right. So I kept moving them. I had to keep moving them into this pattern, this specific grid on the floor and the bench, because I just knew it was the right way they needed to sit. It’s like, the angles have to align perfectly or it doesn't work. And I was... I guess I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I was doing it. The call numbers from the radio, you know? Just saying them over and over, because the numbers anchor the pattern. They lock it in. 

My lieutenant came out and he told me to stop. He was getting loud, telling me to step away from the bags and go up to the office, but I couldn't. I wouldn't step away. He didn't understand that if I stopped, if I broke that sequence before it was finished... it felt like the whole bay would go bad. Like the whole garage, the rigs, the concrete, everything would just spoil or shatter or go completely wrong if I didn't finish the sequence exactly how it was supposed to go. I couldn't let that happen. So I wouldn't stop, and... well, they made me come here.
When you were arranging the airway bags, did part of you realize that the idea that everything would spoil or shatter if you stopped might not actually be true?

No, no, you’re not hearing me. It’s not about whether it’s true or not, it *is* true. I felt it. It’s like a physical weight in the air, you know? Like when the barometric pressure drops before a massive storm and you can feel it in your joints, in your teeth even. That’s what it was like. If I stopped, the whole structure of the place was going to collapse in on itself, just spoil right there on the concrete. And see, the thing is, I had to make sure the bags were right because... well, because I know they’re already trying to build a case against me. 

It’s the injury review people, and some of the supervisors, too. They’re watching me. They’ve got the station cameras—the ones in the bay, the ones by the lockers, even the one near the dispatch desk that’s supposed to be broken, I know it’s not broken. They’re watching every move I make, tracking my sequences, and then they go into the system and they change my triage notes. My paperwork. I’ll write down a perfectly good assessment, standard protocol, ABCs, everything by the book, and then later I’ll look and it’s been altered. They change the vitals I recorded, they change the interventions, just to make it look like I’m unsafe. Like I don’t know what I’m doing. And when I try to bring it up, when I say, "Hey, this isn't what I wrote, someone’s been in my files," they just look at me with these blank faces and tell me it’s just routine paperwork. "Oh, it’s just a system glitch," or "Oh, it’s just routine auditing." Routine! It’s not routine. They’re actively rewriting my reality on paper to make me look incompetent, which is exactly why I couldn't let them interrupt me with the bags. If I let them break the pattern, they win. They get exactly what they want.
Have you been needing much less sleep than usual lately and still feeling full of energy?

No, no, sleep isn't... I mean, I'm sleeping. It's not like I'm staying up for days on end bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I'm getting my rest. Well, as much rest as anyone can get when they work the shifts I do, right? You're on a 24-hour rotation, you're sleeping in the bunk room with one ear open anyway, waiting for the tones to drop. It's a different kind of sleep. You're never really fully out because the radio is always right there on your hip or on the nightstand, and you have to be ready to jump into your boots and be in the rig in under two minutes. 

But lately, even when I'm off shift, even when I'm home in my own bed... I mean, I'm sleeping, but it's not like I wake up feeling like I could run a marathon. I'm tired. I'm actually really, really tired. It's exhausting having to keep track of everything, you know? Watching the cameras, checking my paperwork, making sure the sequences are right... it takes a lot out of you. It's not like I have some kind of endless supply of energy. I wish I did. Honestly, if I had more energy, maybe I could catch them in the act of changing my triage notes. But no, I'm sleeping my usual amount, maybe even a little more when I can, but it doesn't seem to make a dent in how heavy everything feels. It's just a constant, grinding kind of exhaustion, not this full-of-energy thing you're talking about. I'm just... I'm just trying to keep my head above water with all of this going on.
Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?

Voices? Like, people talking when there's nobody in the room? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. I mean, the only voices I hear are the ones I'm supposed to hear, you know? The dispatchers over the radio, my partner complaining about the suspension on the rig, the patients when we're trying to get a history out of them. That's it. It's not like I'm sitting in an empty room having a conversation with a ghost or something. 

I mean, sure, it gets noisy. It gets really loud, actually. But it's a different kind of loud. It's the hum of the fluorescent lights in the bay, which, by the way, they really need to change the ballasts on those things because they have this high-pitched whine that just burrows right into your skull if you stand under them too long. And the tones... you hear the tones in your sleep sometimes, the drop before a call comes in. Any EMT will tell you that. You'll be at the grocery store and hear a beep at the register and your heart rate spikes because you think you're getting a call for a cardiac arrest. That's just part of the job, the way the sounds get stuck in your head. 

But actual voices? Like someone whispering to me or telling me things when I'm alone? No. I don't have that. My problem isn't what I'm hearing, it's what they're doing. It's the paperwork, the cameras, the way they're trying to twist everything I do to make me look bad. I don't need voices in my head when I've got real people actively working against me right there in the station. They're loud enough with their actions, you know? I don't need to hear them talking when nobody's there, because I know exactly what they're saying behind my back anyway.
How long have you been dealing with people watching you and changing your paperwork?

Well, the camera thing and the paperwork... that's been, I'd say, about two months now. Two solid months of this constant... surveillance. It started right around the time we had that bad pile-up on I-95, you know, the one where the tanker rolled? It was chaos, absolute chaos, and we were running non-stop for hours. And right after that, I started noticing the little things. At first, I thought maybe I was just misremembering my own notes because I was so exhausted from that shift, but then it kept happening. 

I'd look at my tablet, and a blood pressure reading I knew for a fact I typed in as 120 over 80 would suddenly say 140 over 90. Or a pulse ox reading would be bumped down just a few points, just enough to make it look like I missed a respiratory issue. It's insidious, really. And the cameras, I started noticing the red lights on them staying on longer, tracking me when I walked across the bay to check the rig's oil. I even tested it once, I took two steps to the left and stopped, and the lens physically panned to follow me. 

So yeah, two months of this. Two months of having to double, triple check every single keystroke, every single form, making sure I have a mental backup of every intervention I perform. And then there's the way they act in the station. It's like they're all in on it, whispering when I walk into the day room, stopping their conversations mid-sentence. That's what really got everyone all worked up and alarmed, you know? They act like *I'm* the one acting strange, but they're the ones orchestrating this whole elaborate setup. It's exhausting, having to be on guard every single second of a 24-hour shift for the last sixty days. You have no idea what it's like to know that your own team, the people you're supposed to trust with your life out on the street, are actively trying to dismantle your career from the inside out.
Before you start repeating the numbers or arranging the bags, do unwanted thoughts pop into your mind that make you feel you have to do it?

Unwanted thoughts? No, it's not like... it's not like a thought pops into my head and says, "Hey, go do this." It's not a suggestion. It's a necessity. It's the sequence. The numbers, the bags... it's all part of the sequence. That's actually why they sent me here, you know. They didn't understand it. I was in the bay, right by the rig, and I had the airway bags out. You know the airway bags? The blue ones, with the intubation kits and the King airways? I had them out, and I was moving them into the pattern. The pattern I knew was right. Because if they aren't in the right pattern, the sequence is broken, and if the sequence is broken, the whole bay goes bad. 

And the numbers, the dispatch numbers... I have to repeat them out loud. It's not an unwanted thought, it's just what has to happen. You repeat the numbers to lock the sequence in place. It's like... it's like setting the parking brake on the rig. You don't just think about setting it, you actually pull the lever so the truck doesn't roll away. Repeating the numbers out loud is pulling the lever. So I was doing that, setting the bags in the pattern, saying the numbers, and my lieutenant—Lieutenant Harris, who, by the way, is definitely one of the ones changing my paperwork—he comes over and tells me to stop. He's yelling at me to step away from the bags. 

But I couldn't step away. I wouldn't do it. I couldn't just stop in the middle of the sequence. If I stopped, the whole bay would go bad. Everything would just... unravel. The calls would go wrong, the rig wouldn't start, the paperwork would get even more twisted up. I had to finish it. So I kept going, putting the bags in the right spots, saying the numbers, and he's getting louder, telling me I'm off the truck, telling me I need a psych eval. That's how I ended up sitting here talking to you. Because they couldn't see that I was actually keeping things from going bad. They just saw me arranging the bags and repeating the numbers and decided I was the problem. But it wasn't an unwanted thought making me do it. It was the only way to keep the sequence intact.
For at least one month in a row, have you been convinced that your supervisors were watching you and changing your paperwork?

A month? Like I was saying before, it’s been at least two solid months of this, every single day. So yes, absolutely for a month in a row. And it’s not just that I’m "convinced" of it, like it's some sort of theory I cooked up. I *know* it for a fact. 

It’s the injury review people, mostly, and a couple of the shift supervisors—Harris being the main one, obviously, but there are others involved too. They sit up there in their offices, or wherever they monitor the feeds from, and they watch me through the station cameras. I told you how the lenses physically track me across the bay, right? They're monitoring every move I make. But the paperwork part, the triage notes... that’s where they’re really trying to build a case against me. 

They go into the system, into the electronic patient care records, after I've already synced my tablet, and they actually change my triage notes. I'll write down exactly what happened—say, a patient was perfectly stable, airway clear, normal vitals—and I'll go back later and the narrative has been altered. They tweak the numbers or change my assessment details just enough to make it look like I missed something critical, like I’m practicing unsafe medicine out on the street. They want to make me look incompetent, like I'm a liability to the department. 

And you want to know the absolute kicker? The craziest part about all of this? When I actually try to bring it up to them, when I point out the discrepancies in the logs and say, "Hey, this isn't what I wrote, someone is messing with my files," they just brush it off. They look me right in the eye, completely deadpan, and tell me it’s just "routine paperwork." They'll say it's just a system update, or an administrative correction, or a quality assurance review. Quality assurance! Can you believe that? They call it routine, but I know exactly what it is. You don't just change an EMT's triage notes for "routine" reasons. That’s a legal document! If a call goes to court, that paperwork is my lifeline. But they don't care about that. They just care about twisting the records to make me look unsafe so they have an excuse to pull my certs and get me off the rig. It's so obvious what they're doing, even when they stand there and lie to my face about it being routine.
For the last month, have these beliefs and the need to do the sequence been present almost every day?

Every single day? Yes. I mean, like I've been trying to tell you, it's not just the last month. It's been two months. Sixty days, give or take, of waking up, putting on my uniform, and knowing the second I step into the bay, it's starting all over again. 

You don't just get to take a day off from it. The camera and paperwork stuff, and the station behavior—you know, the sequence with the bags and the numbers that got everyone so completely alarmed and worked up—all of that has been going on for about the last two months. Every shift. Because it's not like the cameras take a holiday, right? They don't just turn off the feeds on a Sunday. And if I don't do the sequence on a Tuesday, the bay goes bad just as fast as it would on a Friday. I can't just drop my guard for a single afternoon. 

So, yes, every day. Every single day I have to check and re-check my tablet to see what they changed, and every single day I have to make sure the sequence is locked in place so the rig doesn't go bad on us. It’s a constant, heavy weight. You have to understand, when people are watching you that closely, when they are actively trying to dismantle your life, you don't get a break. So it's been two solid months of this, day in and day out, not just one.
Compared with before this started, have you been having trouble doing your job the way you normally could?

Trouble doing my job? Well... yeah. I mean, look where I am. I can't work the ambulance anymore. That's just a fact right now. After the whole thing in the bay with the airway bags and the numbers, they pulled me off the rig. They said I wasn't fit for the street, which is completely backwards because I was the one keeping things from going bad, but whatever. 

So they stuck me on desk duty, right? Like I'm some rookie who twisted an ankle. But even doing that... how am I supposed to do desk-duty notes when the system itself is compromised? I'd do the equipment checks in the back room, I'd write up the logs, and they'd tell me I was being unreliable. They said my notes were unreliable, my checks were unreliable... which is incredibly rich, considering they were the ones actively going into the system and changing my files! But they used that as their excuse. They said I was too unreliable to even sit at a desk, so they just took me completely off the schedule. I have zero shifts. I'm a certified EMT, and I'm not even allowed on the schedule right now. 

And it’s not just the job, either. It bleeds into everything else. You asked about doing things normally... there is no normal anymore. I’ve mostly stopped seeing my friends. I used to go out, maybe grab a beer with some of the guys from the other houses, but I just... I can't do that now. I don't know who's talking to Harris or the injury review people, for one, and I just don't have the energy for it. I’m not even keeping up with things at home the way I used to. The laundry, the dishes, the yard... it all just sits there and piles up. Because when you're dealing with this much pressure, trying to keep the sequences locked in and watching your back because your own department is trying to ruin you, who has the time or the focus to vacuum a rug or sit around at a bar making small talk? You just can't. It takes everything you have. So yeah, I guess you could say I'm having trouble.
Since all of this began, has there ever been any period before these last two months when you had the same kind of beliefs or sequences?

Before these last two months? No. No, never. I mean, you have to understand, I've been doing this job for a long time. I put in the work, I got my degree, I earned my certs... I was a good medic. A really good one. You can't survive out on the street, working a rig in all kinds of chaotic conditions, if you're constantly dealing with this kind of targeted harassment or having to lock down the bay every single shift to keep things safe. It just wouldn't work. 

So before about sixty days ago, everything was... well, it was completely fine. It was normal. I’d show up, do my standard equipment checks, run my calls, sync my tablet at the end of the shift, and go home. That was it. No one was monitoring the security feeds to track my movements across the room. Harris wasn't breathing down my neck or having the injury review board alter my patient care records behind my back. And the sequences... I didn't need to do the sequences with the airway bags and the numbers back then because the bay wasn't going bad. The rig was perfectly safe. 

It’s only been these last two solid months that they started this whole campaign against me, forcing me to take all these precautions just to survive my shift. So, no, there was never any other time in my life, or in my entire career, where I had to deal with anything even remotely like this. It’s completely unprecedented. It's like a switch just flipped in the department two months ago and suddenly I became their primary target, and I've been dealing with it every day since. But before that? Never. Nothing like this at all.
From the very first day this started until today, has all of this lasted less than three months?

Less than three months? No, no, you're getting the timeline mixed up. The camera stuff, the sequences with the bags, me getting pulled off the rig and stuck on desk duty—yes, that specifically has been the last two months. But the actual start of this whole thing? The real beginning of when they started coming after me? That goes back much further. It’s been about eight months. 

See, it all started after I got hurt on the job. About eight months ago, we were doing an ambulance transfer, and it was a mess. I ended up hurting my shoulder and my ribs pretty badly. And you know how it is when you get injured on the job—there's all this paperwork, the injury review board gets involved, workers comp, the whole nine yards. That's when I first noticed things getting weird. That's when Harris and the review people started looking at me differently, like I was a liability or something they needed to get rid of. 

At first, it was subtle, right? Just extra scrutiny, questioning my reports, making me feel like I was exaggerating my shoulder pain. But then it escalated. They started going into my files, messing with my records, trying to build this whole case against me. And then, two months ago, that’s when they really turned up the heat with the cameras and the station behavior, which is when I had to start doing the sequences to keep the bay from going bad. 

So, if you're asking when the whole ordeal began, when the department first turned against me and started this campaign? That was eight months ago, right after the transfer injury. But the really intense stuff, the daily sequences and them completely taking me off the schedule? That’s been the last sixty days. You see how it all connects? It didn't just happen overnight; it’s been this long, drawn-out process of them trying to push me out ever since I messed up my ribs and shoulder.
Have you noticed yourself talking much less than usual or feeling emotionally flat since this started?

Talking less or feeling flat? I mean... yeah, I guess you could say that. But it's more than just feeling flat. It's like... it's like someone pulled the plug on the whole system, you know? Like the battery on the monitor is just dead and no matter how many times you hit the power button, nothing happens. 

Most days now, I just sit in my apartment. Just sit there. I have this... this stack of trays, the tres, just sitting over in the corner of the room. And the food... I've got perfectly good food still sitting in the fridge, but I don't touch it. I used to cook, you know? I used to make these big meals, meal-prep for my shifts, make sure I had good protein for when I was on the rig. But now? The thought of getting up, taking the food out, turning on the stove, standing there... it's just... I can't. I can't get myself to care. I can't get myself to start any of it. 

And talking? Who am I going to talk to? I used to call up the guys, we'd get a pickup game of basketball going at the park down the street. It was a whole thing. But I haven't picked up the phone to call them in... I don't even know how long. I just don't have the words anymore. Or the energy. It's like my brain is so heavy with everything else, with Harris and the sequences and the injury review, that there's no room left for anything else. There's no room for basketball or cooking or just... just being normal. 

So I just sit there. The apartment gets quiet, the trays pile up in the corner, the food sits in the fridge, and I just... I exist. That's all I'm doing right now. Just existing. Because trying to do anything else, trying to care about anything else... it's just too much. It's completely draining. So yeah, I guess emotionally flat is one way to put it, but it really just feels like I'm completely empty.
Since this started, have you found yourself losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

Yeah, I mean, that's exactly what I was just getting at with the basketball and the cooking. It's all gone. The interest, the drive, the... whatever you want to call it. It's just vanished. Like I was saying, most days I really just sit in my apartment. I'll sit on the edge of the couch or just stand there looking at the wall, and I'll see the trays—that stack of them just sitting right there in the corner of the room, gathering dust—and I know I should do something about it. I know I should clean up or, you know, open the fridge where all that perfectly good food is still sitting. 

I bought all these groceries before things got really bad, right? Chicken breasts, vegetables, the whole setup I used to do every Sunday without fail. I used to genuinely love doing that. I'd put on some music, chop everything up, get all my containers lined up for the week so I'd be ready and fueled up for my shifts on the rig. I took a lot of pride in taking care of myself. But now? Now the food is just sitting in there, probably going bad, and I just... I can't get myself to care. I look at the fridge door and the thought of opening it, of pulling out a pan, turning on the burner... it's like staring at a mountain I have to climb with no gear. 

And the guys... man, I used to live for those pickup games. We'd go hard for three, four hours at the park, sweat out all the stress from the calls, maybe grab a drink after. It was the best part of my week, hands down. But I'm not calling them. I haven't called them in I don't even know how long. I don't even look at my phone when it buzzes anymore. I just can't get myself to start anything, you know? It's not even that I'm actively sad about missing basketball or sad about the cooking stopping, it's just this massive, heavy blankness. I just sit there with the trays in the corner and the food in the fridge, and I just don't care about any of the things I used to love. I don't care about any of it anymore.
Have you felt depressed most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

Depressed? I mean... no. Not depressed. I think people get those things confused, you know? The flatness I was just talking about and actual depression. Because being depressed, feeling sad... that's an emotion. That's an active feeling. I remember what that feels like. Years ago, when my dog died, I was depressed. I cried, I felt this literal ache in my chest, I was mourning. But this thing right now? With the apartment and the trays and the food? It's not sadness. 

My mom actually asked me the same thing a while back, before I stopped picking up the phone. She wanted to know if I was depressed about the shoulder injury, or depressed because of what Harris and the review board were doing to my career at the station. And I tried to explain to her that it doesn't feel like that at all. If I was depressed, you would think I'd be sitting on the couch crying about not being on the rig anymore, or getting upset that they pulled me off the schedule and replaced me. But I'm not shedding any tears. I don't feel blue or down in the dumps. 

It is more like... well, think about the ambulance. If the engine is completely blown and making all these horrible grinding noises, that is like being depressed. It is actively hurting. But my situation? It is just like the gas tank is completely empty. There is no gas. No spark. Nothing is grinding because nothing is moving at all. So no, I haven't been depressed for two weeks, or most of the day, or any of that. I am just... unplugged. I don't have the energy to even be sad about it. If you are looking for sadness, it's just not there. It's just a complete blank.
Since all of this first began eight months ago, have these problems been present continuously the whole time?

Continuously? Yeah. Yeah, it hasn't stopped for a single day. It's just been this... this one long, unbroken stretch of exactly what I've been telling you about. I haven't had a single day where I woke up and felt normal or wanted to cook or play basketball. 

And I know exactly when the clock started ticking on all of this, because it was right after the injury. It was about eight months ago. We were on a run, doing this ambulance transfer—which, you know, is usually pretty routine, something I've done a thousand times without even thinking about it, just muscle memory. But the weight shifted, or the angle of the stretcher was wrong, and I had to catch the load abruptly so we wouldn't drop the patient. When I did that, I just completely wrecked myself. I hurt my shoulder really bad, and I messed up my ribs, too. Just a terrible, tearing kind of pain in the shoulder, and my ribs were just screaming every time I tried to take a deep breath. 

That was eight months ago. And ever since that specific transfer, ever since my shoulder and ribs gave out and they had to pull me off the rig... that's exactly when the plug got pulled on everything else. It hasn't let up or given me a break for a minute. Every single day since that ambulance transfer, for eight solid months, it's just been this same heavy, continuous blankness.
For at least one month, have you had almost no motivation to do everyday things like cooking or cleaning?

Yeah, well, I feel like I've been saying that, right? It's been way longer than a month. It's been the whole eight months since the injury. But yeah, definitely for the last month, it's just been exactly what I described. I just... I sit there. I sit on the edge of the couch, or I stand by the window, and I just stare. 

The motivation is completely gone. Zero. It's like I was telling you about the cooking. I used to be so meticulous about it. Sunday afternoons, I'd have the music going, I'd have the cutting board out, chopping the vegetables, grilling the chicken, portioning it all out into those little containers so I'd be ready for my shifts. I took pride in it. I really did. But now? Now the food is just sitting in the fridge. It's probably rotting in there right now. I know it's in there, and I know I should do something with it, but the thought of opening the door, getting a pan out, turning on the stove... it's just impossible. I can't get myself to care enough to even try. 

And it's the same with cleaning. You should see my place. I mentioned those trays earlier, right? There's just this stack of trays sitting in the corner of the room. They've been there for I don't know how long, just gathering dust. Any normal person would just pick them up and put them away or throw them out, but I just look at them. I look at them and I know I should clean them up, but I don't. I can't start. 

And the basketball, too. I haven't called the guys for pickup games in months. We used to go hard for hours at the park, sweat it all out, but now my phone buzzes and I don't even look at it. It's not that I'm sitting around crying about missing the games or missing my meal prep routine. It's just that I literally cannot get myself to start anything. Everyday things, the things that used to make up my whole life... I just don't have the drive to do any of it anymore. It's all just sitting there, like the trays in the corner and the food in the fridge, and I just sit there with it, not doing a damn thing.

patient.answer:
Well, it wasn’t my idea to come here, I’ll tell you that right now. I’ve been on the trucks for years, I'm an EMT, and you get to know how the equipment has to be, how it breathes, almost. But my lieutenant... they, uh, they sent me here because of what happened at the station. 

I was down in the bay, right? And the airway bags—the ones we use for intubation and oxygen, they have all the non-rebreather masks and the O2 tanks in them—they just weren't right. So I kept moving them. I had to keep moving them into this pattern, this specific grid on the floor and the bench, because I just knew it was the right way they needed to sit. It’s like, the angles have to align perfectly or it doesn't work. And I was... I guess I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I was doing it. The call numbers from the radio, you know? Just saying them over and over, because the numbers anchor the pattern. They lock it in. 

My lieutenant came out and he told me to stop. He was getting loud, telling me to step away from the bags and go up to the office, but I couldn't. I wouldn't step away. He didn't understand that if I stopped, if I broke that sequence before it was finished... it felt like the whole bay would go bad. Like the whole garage, the rigs, the concrete, everything would just spoil or shatter or go completely wrong if I didn't finish the sequence exactly how it was supposed to go. I couldn't let that happen. So I wouldn't stop, and... well, they made me come here.

inference.note: Initial differential added OCD with mixed obsessions/compulsions as leading possibility based on repetitive arranging and number repetition to neutralize feared catastrophe; also keeping psychotic-spectrum disorders, manic episode with psychotic symptoms, schizoaffective disorder, and obsessive-compulsive personality traits due to possible overvalued/bizarre beliefs and poor ability to disengage.

patient.answer:
No, no, you’re not hearing me. It’s not about whether it’s true or not, it *is* true. I felt it. It’s like a physical weight in the air, you know? Like when the barometric pressure drops before a massive storm and you can feel it in your joints, in your teeth even. That’s what it was like. If I stopped, the whole structure of the place was going to collapse in on itself, just spoil right there on the concrete. And see, the thing is, I had to make sure the bags were right because... well, because I know they’re already trying to build a case against me. 

It’s the injury review people, and some of the supervisors, too. They’re watching me. They’ve got the station cameras—the ones in the bay, the ones by the lockers, even the one near the dispatch desk that’s supposed to be broken, I know it’s not broken. They’re watching every move I make, tracking my sequences, and then they go into the system and they change my triage notes. My paperwork. I’ll write down a perfectly good assessment, standard protocol, ABCs, everything by the book, and then later I’ll look and it’s been altered. They change the vitals I recorded, they change the interventions, just to make it look like I’m unsafe. Like I don’t know what I’m doing. And when I try to bring it up, when I say, "Hey, this isn't what I wrote, someone’s been in my files," they just look at me with these blank faces and tell me it’s just routine paperwork. "Oh, it’s just a system glitch," or "Oh, it’s just routine auditing." Routine! It’s not routine. They’re actively rewriting my reality on paper to make me look incompetent, which is exactly why I couldn't let them interrupt me with the bags. If I let them break the pattern, they win. patient.answer:
No, no, sleep isn't... I mean, I'm sleeping. It's not like I'm staying up for days on end bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I'm getting my rest. Well, as much rest as anyone can get when they work the shifts I do, right? You're on a 24-hour rotation, you're sleeping in the bunk room with one ear open anyway, waiting for the tones to drop. It's a different kind of sleep. You're never really fully out because the radio is always right there on your hip or on the nightstand, and you have to be ready to jump into your boots and be in the rig in under two minutes. 

But lately, even when I'm off shift, even when I'm home in my own bed... I mean, I'm sleeping, but it's not like I wake up feeling like I could run a marathon. I'm tired. I'm actually really, really tired. It's exhausting having to keep track of everything, you know? Watching the cameras, checking my paperwork, making sure the sequences are right... it takes a lot out of you. It's not like I have some kind of endless supply of energy. I wish I did. Honestly, if I had more energy, maybe I could catch them in the act of changing my triage notes. But no, I'm sleeping my usual amount, maybe even a little more when I can, but it doesn't seem to make a dent in how heavy everything feels. It's just a constant, grinding kind of exhaustion, not this full-of-energy thing you're talking about. I'm just... I'm just trying to keep my head above water with all of this going on.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient is experiencing hallucinations, which would help distinguish a primary psychotic disorder from obsessive-compulsive disorder with poor insight.
doctor.question: Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about auditory hallucinations (hearing voices), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Voices? Like, people talking when there's nobody in the room? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. I mean, the only voices I hear are the ones I'm supposed to hear, you know? The dispatchers over the radio, my partner complaining about the suspension on the rig, the patients when we're trying to get a history out of them. That's it. It's not like I'm sitting in an empty room having a conversation with a ghost or something. 

I mean, sure, it gets noisy. It gets really loud, actually. But it's a different kind of loud. It's the hum of the fluorescent lights in the bay, which, by the way, they really need to change the ballasts on those things because they have this high-pitched whine that just burrows right into your skull if you stand under them too long. And the tones... you hear the tones in your sleep sometimes, the drop before a call comes in. Any EMT will tell you that. You'll be at the grocery store and hear a beep at the register and your heart rate spikes because you think you're getting a call for a cardiac arrest. That's just part of the job, the way the sounds get stuck in your head. 

But actual voices? Like someone whispering to me or telling me things when I'm alone? No. I don't have that. My problem isn't what I'm hearing, it's what they're doing. It's the paperwork, the cameras, the way they're trying to twist everything I do to make me look bad. I don't need voices in my head when I've got real people actively working against me right there in the station. They're loud enough with their actions, you know? Well, the camera thing and the paperwork... that's been, I'd say, about two months now. Two solid months of this constant... surveillance. It started right around the time we had that bad pile-up on I-95, you know, the one where the tanker rolled? It was chaos, absolute chaos, and we were running non-stop for hours. It's exhausting, having to be on guard every single second of a 24-hour shift for the last sixty days. Most days now, I just sit in my apartment. Just sit there. I have this... this stack of trays, the tres, just sitting over in the corner of the room. And the food... I've got perfectly good food still sitting in the fridge, but I don't touch it. I used to cook, you know? I used to make these big meals, meal-prep for my shifts, make sure I had good protein for when I was on the rig. But now? The thought of getting up, taking the food out, turning on the stove, standing there... it's just... I can't. I can't get myself to care. I can't get myself to start any of it. 

And talking? Who am I going to talk to? I used to call up the guys, we'd get a pickup game of basketball going at the park down the street. It was a whole thing. But I haven't picked up the phone to call them in... I don't even know how long. I just don't have the words anymore. Or the energy. It's like my brain is so heavy with everything else, with Harris and the sequences and the injury review, that there's no room left for anything else. There's no room for basketball or cooking or just... just being normal. 

So I just sit there. The apartment gets quiet, the trays pile up in the corner, the food sits in the fridge, and I just... I exist. That's all I'm doing right now. Just existing. Because trying to do anything else, trying to care about anything else... it's just too much. It's completely draining. So yeah, I guess emotionally flat is one way to put it, but it really just feels like I'm completely empty.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent negative symptoms, which would favor schizophrenia over delusional disorder or brief psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Since this started, have you found yourself losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Most days I just sit in my apartment with the tres in the corner and food still in the fridge, not calling the guys for basketball or cooking like I used to, because I can't get myself to care or start anything.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities (anhedonia/apathy), which is a key component of negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean, that's exactly what I was just getting at with the basketball and the cooking. It's all gone. The interest, the drive, the... whatever you want to call it. It's just vanished. Like I was saying, most days I really just sit in my apartment. I'll sit on the edge of the couch or just stand there looking at the wall, and I'll see the trays—that stack of them just sitting right there in the corner of the room, gathering dust—and I know I should do something about it. I know I should clean up or, you know, open the fridge where all that perfectly good food is still sitting. 

I bought all these groceries before things got really bad, right? Chicken breasts, vegetables, the whole setup I used to do every Sunday without fail. I used to genuinely love doing that. I'd put on some music, chop everything up, get all my containers lined up for the week so I'd be ready and fueled up for my shifts on the rig. I took a lot of pride in taking care of myself. But now? Now the food is just sitting in there, probably going bad, and I just... I can't get myself to care. I look at the fridge door and the thought of opening it, of pulling out a pan, turning on the burner... it's like staring at a mountain I have to climb with no gear. 

And the guys... man, I used to live for those pickup games. We'd go hard for three, four hours at the park, sweat out all the stress from the calls, maybe grab a drink after. It was the best part of my week, hands down. But I'm not calling them. I haven't called them in I don't even know how long. I don't even look at my phone when it buzzes anymore. I just can't get myself to start anything, you know? It's not even that I'm actively sad about missing basketball or sad about the cooking stopping, it's just this massive, heavy blankness. I just sit there with the trays in the corner and the food in the fridge, and I just don't care about any of the things I used to love. I don't care about any of it anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine whether a major depressive episode has been present for at least two weeks, which would distinguish schizophrenia from delusional or brief psychotic disorder by clarifying mood syndrome prominence/duration.
doctor.question: Have you felt depressed most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Depressed? I mean... no. Not depressed. I think people get those things confused, you know? The flatness I was just talking about and actual depression. Because being depressed, feeling sad... that's an emotion. That's an active feeling. I remember what that feels like. Years ago, when my dog died, I was depressed. I cried, I felt this literal ache in my chest, I was mourning. But this thing right now? With the apartment and the trays and the food? It's not sadness. 

My mom actually asked me the same thing a while back, before I stopped picking up the phone. She wanted to know if I was depressed about the shoulder injury, or depressed because of what Harris and the review board were doing to my career at the station. And I tried to explain to her that it doesn't feel like that at all. If I was depressed, you would think I'd be sitting on the couch crying about not being on the rig anymore, or getting upset that they pulled me off the schedule and replaced me. But I'm not shedding any tears. I don't feel blue or down in the dumps. 

It is more like... well, think about the ambulance. If the engine is completely blown and making all these horrible grinding noises, that is like being depressed. It is actively hurting. But my situation? It is just like the gas tank is completely empty. There is no gas. No spark. Nothing is grinding because nothing is moving at all. So no, I haven't been depressed for two weeks, or most of the day, or any of that. I am just... unplugged. I don't have the energy to even be sad about it. If you are looking for sadness, it's just not there. It's just a complete blank.

inference.note: Removed F23 because symptoms have persisted beyond 3 months when counting the persecutory beliefs from their onset (~8 months). Added prominent negative symptoms/anhedonia/avolition and functional decline, which favor F20.0 over F22, though delusional disorder remains possible if negative symptoms are secondary.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been at least six months of continuous disturbance, which would favor schizophrenia over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Since all of this first began eight months ago, have these problems been present continuously the whole time?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This all started after I hurt my shoulder and ribs during that ambulance transfer about eight months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline and continuous presence of the problems since they started eight months ago, which corresponds to the overall duration of the illness.

patient.answer:
Continuously? Yeah. Yeah, it hasn't stopped for a single day. It's just been this... this one long, unbroken stretch of exactly what I've been telling you about. I haven't had a single day where I woke up and felt normal or wanted to cook or play basketball. 

And I know exactly when the clock started ticking on all of this, because it was right after the injury. It was about eight months ago. We were on a run, doing this ambulance transfer—which, you know, is usually pretty routine, something I've done a thousand times without even thinking about it, just muscle memory. But the weight shifted, or the angle of the stretcher was wrong, and I had to catch the load abruptly so we wouldn't drop the patient. When I did that, I just completely wrecked myself. I hurt my shoulder really bad, and I messed up my ribs, too. Just a terrible, tearing kind of pain in the shoulder, and my ribs were just screaming every time I tried to take a deep breath. 

That was eight months ago. And ever since that specific transfer, ever since my shoulder and ribs gave out and they had to pull me off the rig... that's exactly when the plug got pulled on everything else. It hasn't let up or given me a break for a minute. Every single day since that ambulance transfer, for eight solid months, it's just been this same heavy, continuous blankness.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there have been prominent negative symptoms such as avolition or diminished emotional expression lasting at least one month, which would favor schizophrenia over delusional disorder.
doctor.question: For at least one month, have you had almost no motivation to do everyday things like cooking or cleaning?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: Most days I just sit in my apartment with the tres in the corner and food still in the fridge, not calling the guys for basketball or cooking like I used to, because I can't get myself to care or start anything.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a lack of motivation to do everyday tasks like cooking or cleaning, which corresponds to negative symptoms (avolition).

patient.answer:
Yeah, well, I feel like I've been saying that, right? It's been way longer than a month. It's been the whole eight months since the injury. But yeah, definitely for the last month, it's just been exactly what I described. I just... I sit there. I sit on the edge of the couch, or I stand by the window, and I just stare. 

The motivation is completely gone. Zero. It's like I was telling you about the cooking. I used to be so meticulous about it. Sunday afternoons, I'd have the music going, I'd have the cutting board out, chopping the vegetables, grilling the chicken, portioning it all out into those little containers so I'd be ready for my shifts. I took pride in it. I really did. But now? Now the food is just sitting in the fridge. It's probably rotting in there right now. I know it's in there, and I know I should do something with it, but the thought of opening the door, getting a pan out, turning on the stove... it's just impossible. I can't get myself to care enough to even try. 

And it's the same with cleaning. You should see my place. I mentioned those trays earlier, right? There's just this stack of trays sitting in the corner of the room. They've been there for I don't know how long, just gathering dust. Any normal person would just pick them up and put them away or throw them out, but I just look at them. I look at them and I know I should clean them up, but I don't. I can't start. 

And the basketball, too. I haven't called the guys for pickup games in months. We used to go hard for hours at the park, sweat it all out, but now my phone buzzes and I don't even look at it. It's not that I'm sitting around crying about missing the games or missing my meal prep routine. It's just that I literally cannot get myself to start anything. Everyday things, the things that used to make up my whole life... I just don't have the drive to do any of it anymore. It's all just sitting there, like the trays in the corner and the food in the fridge, and I just sit there with it, not doing a damn thing.

inference.note: Negative symptoms (marked avolition/anhedonia/alogia/flatness) have been continuous for 8 months, with persecutory and bizarre delusions plus disorganized/catatonic-like repetitive behavior; total duration >6 months rules out F22 delusional disorder and supports schizophrenia, paranoid subtype.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent persecutory delusions and bizarre/delusional beliefs about sequences preventing collapse, with marked decline in work and social functioning. Negative symptoms are also present, including avolition, diminished speech/social withdrawal, affective flattening/emptiness, and loss of interest. Symptoms have been continuous for about 8 months, meeting duration for schizophrenia and arguing against brief or acute psychotic disorders. Mania and primary depressive syndrome were not supported.
